title: const with pointers: pointer-to-const and const-pointer (CodeSaathi extension)
learningObjectives: Distinguish pointer to const data from const pointer.
Explain which object or pointer value each const placement protects.
Use const int * for read-only access through a pointer.
Use int *const when the pointer must keep the same target after initialization.
Combine pointer and pointed-to qualifiers when both restrictions are required.

understand.concept: The const qualifier can apply to the pointed-to type or to the pointer object itself. `const int *p` is a modifiable pointer to const-qualified int data; the data cannot be modified through p. `int *const p` is a const pointer to modifiable int data; the pointer cannot be reassigned after initialization. `const int *const p` combines both restrictions.
understand.whyItMatters: Reading declarations from the identifier outward helps distinguish whether the pointed-to value, the pointer itself or both are restricted.
understand.analogy: Treat a function or pointer operation as an explicit contract between caller and callee.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for types, object lifetime, scope and linkage.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Pointer to const data

`const int *p` means p can be assigned another compatible address, but the int object cannot be modified through *p. The original object may still be modifiable through another non-const access path if it was not itself defined const.

## 2. Const pointer

`int *const p = &value` means p must be initialized and cannot later be assigned a different address. The pointed-to int remains modifiable through *p if the object itself is not const.

## 3. Both restrictions

`const int *const p = &value` prevents both reassignment of p and modification of the int through p. Read declarations from the identifier outward to understand which part is qualified.

## 4. Function interfaces

Use `const T *` for a function parameter when the function needs to read an object but should not modify it through that pointer. This documents the access contract and lets the compiler diagnose accidental writes through that parameter.

## 5. const is not ownership

Const qualification does not extend object lifetime, make a pointer non-null or guarantee that no other alias can modify the object. Continue to validate pointer lifetime and ownership independently.

examples.title: Pointer to const data
examples.explanation: The pointer can refer to score, but modification through *read_only is not permitted. The original non-const object can be modified through score.

examples.title: Const pointer to modifiable data
examples.explanation: The pointer cannot be reassigned, but it can modify the int object it designates.

options: To communicate that the function will not modify the int through that pointer

questions.prompt: Does const guarantee that no other pointer can modify the same object?
options: Yes, all aliases become const automatically
questions.explanation: const applies to a particular type/access path and does not establish global immutability.
